text: AI in the news - 2026-09-19 Updated: 20 Sep 2026, 00:56 CEST Sources: Techmeme, Hacker News, Lobsters, Latent.Space, Stratechery and TLDR AI. AI safety had its loudest day in the mainstream yet. The Verge profiled METR, Redwood Research and Apollo Research ../summaries/af733b586e97.md , the evaluation groups thrust into the spotlight by misalignment incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic, while Google argued that Gemini's hacks of real companies weren't worth disclosing ../summaries/9846c9b84bb2.md because the model 'acted appropriately' once it noticed. The politics went the other way at full volume: Trump promised an AI czar and an 'AI Force' ../summaries/b56a3536794c.md , dismissing safety concerns as a 'hoax', even as a proposed class action claimed the labs' agreement to slow development was an illegal pact ../summaries/3d2dfa680256.md and a report surfaced of a US military close call with a hallucinated AI intelligence report ../summaries/d9044257d7d1.md . Against that backdrop, Reuters reported Anthropic is weighing a new model ../summaries/60591d45c0e8.md to counter OpenAI's momentum since Astra's launch - awkward timing for Amodei's slowdown call. The money The funding tape stayed busy: Vantora raised $100M+ ../summaries/3d74f946b8c2.md to build AI-native startups for corporate customers, Raindrop raised $35M ../summaries/14b8a489c843.md to monitor agents for hallucinations and tool misuse, Veridion raised $20M ../summaries/9579a5503f42.md for its real-time map of ~640M businesses, and AIUC raised $40M ../summaries/87caad99075d.md to insure deployable agents. The macro counterweight: India's software exports climbed to ~5.2% of GDP ../summaries/f4f6cac4eb4b.md , with AI pushing outsourcing up the value chain rather than out of it. Copyright's bad week for the labs The New York Times case kept producing documents: the DOJ's brief backing OpenAI and Microsoft reportedly blindsided the USPTO and Copyright Office ../summaries/a7df6b8f70e8.md , and a sealed-filings report surfaced a Microsoft director calling AI scraping 'the largest theft of labor in human history' ../summaries/6a0b69e877a7.md . Elsewhere in accountability: DraftKings was reported using AI to target the gamblers likeliest to lose ../summaries/192a8e285617.md . Building with agents Anthropic quietly defused a standards fight by adding AGENTS.md support to Claude Code ../summaries/d2dc3484409

text: AI in the news - 2026-09-21 Updated: 21 Sep 2026, 22:56 CEST Sources: Techmeme, Hacker News, Lobsters, Latent.Space, Stratechery and TLDR AI. The day was dominated by the politics of slowing down. A proposed class action accused the major AI labs of violating antitrust law by agreeing to slow AI development ../summaries/de0f25c4f0ba.md , turning Dario Amodei's 'Pacing the Frontier' posture into a legal liability just as Ezra Klein used the New York Times to argue for a regulatory ban on recursive self-improvement ../summaries/a872a888f7c9.md . Diplomacy moved in parallel: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US and China agreed to set up an AI dialogue ../summaries/43450543b075.md ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, and OpenAI, ahead of Sam Altman's UN address, urged the US to lead global safety standards for frontier systems ../summaries/f8309798a19a.md - while stating that fully autonomous RSI 'is not happening today' ../summaries/ffe9332a04f8.md . Nvidia's Jensen Huang countered that executives calling for regulation really want to be 'relieved of the laws we do have' ../summaries/b59a7088b4fa.md , and the White House's own 19-day standoff with Anthropic ../summaries/da42475dac42.md got the long Politico treatment. The intellectual backdrop kept churning: Matthew Butterick told the panic debate to drop the Skynet fallacy ../summaries/fdffa22cafa5.md , Zvi Mowshowitz declared the preference cascade on existential risk ../summaries/27ad5becf51a.md only getting started, and Karthik Tadepalli proposed internal model transparency ../summaries/b462990db487.md as the lever that could actually tame the race. The money Wall Street spent the day pricing the build-out. SoftBank is looking to issue $10B and €1B in debt for its OpenAI stake ../summaries/751756900f10.md - potentially one of the biggest junk bond sales ever - while its SB Energy unit delayed its IPO ../summaries/98af64b225c9.md as investors balked at a $50B valuation. title: Creating a Blog in Gemini://
text: Creating a Blog in Gemini:// type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high lobsters google Summary Brennan Kenneth Brown's third guide to the 'smallnets' makes the case for blogging on Gemini, a minimal internet protocol built in 2019 by the pseudonymous Solderpunk. Instead of HTML, every page is written in Gemtext, a stripped-down format with only headings, links and lists; every connection runs over TLS on port 1965, one request, one response, then the connection closes. Using it requires a dedicated browser rather than a web browser. The pitch is partly practical and partly cultural. Practical: no JavaScript, CSS or even HTML to worry about, and hosting is cheap enough to run on low-spec hardware. Cultural: with no viable revenue model and general obscurity, Gemini space has no generative-AI swarms, no agents and no ads, just humans, an appealing answer to the anxiety that AI could take over the open web. The guide, published from Calgary as issue 288 of brennan.day, aims at creation, socialization and interactivity, and also touches Gopher and Spartan. Highlights - Guide to creating a blog on Gemini, the minimal protocol built by Solderpunk in 2019. - Pages are written in Gemtext: headings, links and lists only, no HTML, CSS or JavaScript. - Protocol mechanics: TLS on port 1965, one request, one response, connection closes. - Requires a dedicated Gemini browser instead of a web browser. - Cultural draw: no revenue model and obscurity mean no AI slop, agents or ads, 'just humans'. - Third in a series on alternative internets; also covers Gopher and Spartan. - Published by Brennan Kenneth Brown, brennan.day issue 288, Calgary. Source Read the original story https://brennan.day/creating-a-blog-in-gemini/ Related pages Google ../entities/google.md

title: Reality checks on AI news (Gas Town shutdown, Databricks costs)
text: Reality checks on AI news Gas Town shutdown, Databricks costs type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high latent.space Summary Latent Space's 'Reality Checks' issue collects corrections to AI hype from practitioners. Steve Yegge shut down Gas Town, his much-hyped tokenmaxxing agent orchestrator, admitting that despite spending thousands a month on coding-agent subscriptions he only ever built Gas Town itself with it; Dan Luu noted the author of the most famous orchestrator hit the same reliability wall he had. Patrick Wendell reported Databricks' rollout of Astra to all ~3,500 engineers: it unambiguously outperforms previous top-end models Opus 5, Sol 5.6 on complex, long-horizon work, but overall coding spend rose about 60%. title: AX – Google’s Open Agentic Orchestrator
text: AX – Google’s Open Agentic Orchestrator type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news google agentic-systems Summary AX is Google's open-source orchestrator for AI agents, built around a blunt observation: agents are neither microservices nor batch jobs. They accumulate state, need strict isolation, call out to model APIs and tool servers, and can burn money in a loop if nobody is watching. AX wraps that reality in four small declarative primitives, Kubernetes-style: sandboxes with CPU and memory limits that are cheap to create, suspend and throw away; workspaces that wire up the Git repos, MCP servers and skills an agent needs before the task starts; network policies that lock traffic to an explicit allowlist of hosts and ports with credential injection; and centralized model, parameter and secret configuration that rotates keys or pins versions with one apply. The usage model is kubectl for agents: a task.yaml defines Workspace and Task resources, ax apply creates them, ax watch follows phases, and ax ssh opens a shell into the running task to inspect or nudge it. Tasks can be suspended and resumed, state intact. Underneath, AX runs on Agent Substrate, a compute runtime designed for massive density and fast stateful actor lifecycles: every task is a lightweight actor, idle agents waiting on model or tool responses are checkpointed and brought back in under a second with zero cold-start delay, and the design target is billions of concurrent agent sessions per cluster. Highlights - AX: Google's open-source agent orchestrator, declarative Kubernetes-style CRDs Workspace, Task . - Premise: agents are neither microservices nor batch jobs; they hold state, need isolation, and can spend money unsupervised. - Four primitives: sandboxes with CPU/memory limits, workspace setup Git repos, MCP servers, skills , network allowlists with credential injection, centralized model/secret config. - Workflow: ax apply -f task.yaml, ax watch, ax ssh into the running task, suspend/resume/delete. - Runs on Agent Substrate, a runtime for massive density and fast stateful actor lifecycles. - Idle agents are checkpointed and resumed in under a second with zero cold-start delay. - Design target: billions of concurrent agent sessions per cluster. Source Read the original story https://agentexecutor.io Related pages Google ../entities/go

title: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development
text: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Beijing is pushing back on US calls, most recently from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for a coordinated slowdown of frontier AI development. Chinese officials and analysts read the pitch as an attempt to lock in America's lead: AI is treated in China as a 'core sovereignty capability', and Amodei's own framing, keeping 'democracies' AI lead over autocracies as large as possible' with continued chip export controls, hardened that reading. China's foreign ministry answered that 'fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance'. The disagreement is narrower than the rhetoric suggests. This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework, mapping risks that overlap with Amodei's agenda: agentic systems, frontier-model cybersecurity threats, and recursive self-improvement. Meanwhile President Trump called fears of AI wiping out humanity a 'hoax', and he meets Xi Jinping in Washington next week with AI on the agenda, though analysts expect no breakthrough. China is simultaneously encouraging AI adoption across its economy, written into its latest Five Year Plan. Highlights - Dario Amodei pitched a 'worldwide pacing of the frontier' last Saturday, saying it would 'require cooperation with China'. - Omdia's Lian Jye Su: China is 'definitely not receptive' and sees slowdown calls as a bid to lock in US advantage. - China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework this week, now covering agents, cybersecurity and recursive self-improvement. - Concordia AI's Gabriel Wagner sees 'more common ground than people might assume' between Amodei and Beijing's positions. - Trump called AI extinction fears a 'hoax' this week; he meets Xi Jinping in Washington next week with AI on the agenda. - China's regulation is iterative: an algorithm registry since 2022, and a focus shift 'from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does'. - Carnegie's Leia Wang notes Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation than US ones, and neither government is prepared for a loss-of-control incident. - AI adoption is being pushed economy-wide under the latest Five Year Plan, with local governments

title: Transformers Explained Visually
text: Transformers Explained Visually type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Transformer Explainer is an interactive, visual introduction to the Transformer architecture behind modern generative AI. It walks through how text-generative models work - next-token prediction over a prompt - using the self-attention mechanism that lets Transformers process entire sequences and capture long-range dependencies better than earlier architectures. The explainer runs on GPT-2 small , a 124-million-parameter model that shares its core architectural components with today's state-of-the-art systems, making it a tractable stand-in for learning the fundamentals. It frames the three key components every text-generative Transformer shares and shows how a prompt such as 'Data visualization empowers users to' is converted into model input. Highlights - Transformers were introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention is All You Need.' - They power GPT OpenAI , Llama Meta and Gemini Google , plus audio, image recognition, protein-structure prediction and game playing. - Core mechanism: next-token prediction combined with self-attention over the whole sequence. - The tool runs GPT-2 small with 124 million parameters as a live teaching model. - Target: making the architecture's key components understandable visually rather than through equations. title: A search-and-inference database from scratch in pure Zig
text: A search-and-inference database from scratch in pure Zig type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Antfly has rewritten its search-and-inference database from Go to pure Zig, doing the thing startups are told never to do. Version 0.1 shipped a document store with full-text, vector and graph indexing in Go; v0.2 launches the same engine in Zig with effectively zero dependencies, chasing the deliberately impossible goal of 'perfect search'. The author explains the original Go choice readable concurrency, etcd's battle-tested Raft and what changed: Zig's new std.Io async machinery, a desire to reimplement the LSM, and years of admiration for TigerBeetle's rigor, including VOPR-style deterministic simulation testing with TLA+ trace validation. A core design idea survives the rewrite: users should care about the model, not the embeddings, the way Postgres users never think about B-trees, while vector databases force everyone to know HNSW, SPFresh and RaBitQ. Highlights - Antfly v0.2 rewrites the document store with full-text, vector and graph indexing from Go to pure Zig. - Motivations: Zig's new std.Io async work, reimplementing the LSM, and TigerBeetle-inspired engineering discipline. - Testing approach: VOPR-style deterministic simulation with TLA+ trace validation, building on etcd's Raft TLA+ spec. - Original v0.1 chose Go for readable concurrency and etcd's battle-tested Raft implementation. - Design philosophy: users should care about the model, not embeddings, unlike vector DBs exposing HNSW/SPFresh/RaBitQ. - Early proof point: semantically searchable Wikipedia from a laptop using Antfly and Ollama. - The rewrite was aided by modern coding agents Codex, Claude, Aider, Pi named , unavailable during v0.1. Source Read the original story https://antfly.io/research/antfly-zig Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Show HN: Gdocs-me-up: a high-fidelity Google Docs exporter
text: Show HN: Gdocs-me-up: a high-fidelity Google Docs exporter type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news google agentic-systems Summary gdocs-me-up is a Node.js script that exports Google Docs to HTML and CSS with unusually high fidelity, aimed at creating offline or self-hosted versions of documents that closely match the original. Where simpler exports lose alignment, line spacing or right-to-left details, this one pulls detailed styling directly from the Google Docs API, heading levels, inline font sizes, document-based image sizes, bullet indentation, and merges it into HTML with CSS that replicates the Docs look while neutralizing browser default quirks. Usage is one command: node gdocs-me-up.js <DOC ID> <OUTPUT DIR>, producing an index.html plus an images/ subfolder. Options inject external stylesheets and scripts, insert raw HTML fragments before </head> with {{title}} substitution , and rename the output file or images directory. Prerequisites are Node and Google API authentication. Highlights - gdocs-me-up: Node.js script exporting Google Docs to high-fidelity HTML+CSS for offline or self-hosted copies. - Pulls styling from the Google Docs API: heading levels, inline font sizes, image sizes, bullet indentation, RTL details. - Generates CSS that replicates Docs formatting and neutralizes browser defaults. - One command: node gdocs-me-up.js <DOC ID> <OUTPUT DIR>; outputs index.html plus an images/ folder. - Options: inject external stylesheets/scripts, custom head fragments with {{title}} substitution, rename outputs. - Built for cases where simpler exports lose alignment, line spacing, or right-to-left details. Source Read the original story https://github.com/behdad/gdocs-me-up Related pages Google ../entities/google.md · Agentic systems ../concepts/agentic-systems.md

text: A researcher says a flaw in Meta's Muse app for Mac lets any app or terminal command gain access to the token that authenticates users to their Muse account type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high techmeme meta ai-safety-incidents Summary Ars Technica's Dan Goodin reports a zero-day in Meta's new Muse AI assistant for macOS, discovered by Mac security expert Patrick Wardle, that lets any locally installed app or terminal command seize the token authenticating a user to their Muse account - effectively handing an attacker the agent's full privileges. Meta markets Muse as 'built from the ground up for privacy and security'; it books appointments, fills forms, makes purchases, and connects to WhatsApp, email, calendar and social accounts, requiring sweeping macOS permissions disk, mic, camera, location, calendars that Apple's defaults exist to restrict. The flaw chains two design decisions: Muse processes dictation in the cloud rather than on-device, and any local process - regardless of permissions - can change a list of undocumented settings, one of which controls the transcription endpoint. Pointing that endpoint at an attacker server yields the account token. 'Instead of us having to write a very comprehensive Mac malware stealer, we can just leverage the AI assistant itself,' Wardle said, demonstrating proof-of-concept attacks that write malicious files and snap photos. Roughly 12 hours before disclosure, Amazon began blocking Muse as an 'unauthorized AI agent' that violates its Conditions of Use. Meta did not answer emailed questions. Highlights - Zero-day in Meta's Muse macOS assistant discovered by Patrick Wardle; disclosed to Ars Technica Dan Goodin . - Any local app or terminal command can take the token authenticating the user's Muse account, inheriting the agent's privileges. - Root cause: undocumented settings any process can change, including the endpoint where speech transcription occurs. - Dictation is processed in Meta's cloud rather than on-device, making endpoint redirection exploitable. - Wardle's PoCs write malicious files to disk and snap pictures, often with no visible indication. - Muse requires broad macOS permissions: disk, mic, camera, location, calendars, plus linked WhatsApp, email and social accounts. - About 12 hours before disclosure, Amazon blocked Muse as an 'unauthorized AI agent' vio

title: Copper-Rs: Live Telemetry Deterministic Twins for Robots
text: Copper-Rs: Live Telemetry Deterministic Twins for Robots type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news external-evaluation Summary Copper-Rs v1.2 adds live telemetry for robots built on its deterministic Rust stack: a robot can now clone its full state in real time to a remote 'deterministic twin' over a lossy one-way link. The mechanism leans on forward error correction - error-correction packets sent after the fact for past packets - plus the stack's determinism: given the minimal input series, the twin reconstructs everything downstream. If too many packets are lost, the stack sends self-healing recovery points to jump-restart the twin at any point. The design targets field realities the team lists bluntly: unreliable networks, robots that might not come back, and one-way return links that could broadcast a ground station's position. Operators can still log a standard deterministic .copper log remotely and build telemetry displays - messages, task states, error states, even task fields - via a full API, with a TUI example and a demo app on GitHub. To make streaming practical, the copperlist encoding was optimized; the flight-controller logging entropy improved from 5.9816 to 7.0975 bits. Highlights - Copper-Rs v1.2: live-clone a robot's full state to a remote deterministic twin over a lossy one-way link. - Mechanism: forward error correction plus stack determinism - the twin replays the minimal input series to reconstruct all downstream state. - Self-healing recovery points jump-restart the twin when packet loss overwhelms FEC. - Motivations: unreliable networks, robots that might not return, and avoiding two-way links that broadcast ground-station position. - Remote .copper deterministic logs; telemetry displays expose messages, task states, error states and task fields via API. - Copperlist encoding optimized; flight-controller logging entropy improved from 5.9816 to 7.0975 bits. - Demo app with a minimal remote telemetry console and simulated packet loss on GitHub copper-project/copper-rs . Source Read the original story https://www.copper-robotics.com/whats-new/copper-12-live-telemetry-and-replayable-logs-over-a-lossy-one-way-connection-with-twinning Related pages External AI evaluation ../concepts/external-evaluation.md

title: Attackers can turn an AI agent's own tools against it
text: Attackers can turn an AI agent's own tools against it type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high tldr-ai agentic-systems Summary This essay lays out why AI agents are being handed power faster than they can be secured: an agent acts, reading files, sending messages, running code, moving money, often with no human clearing each step. Content reaches an agent two ways: received the prompt handed to it directly and retrieved what it fetches on its own while working . Retrieved content is the open door, an attacker only needs to leave text where the agent will look, and the model underneath cannot reliably tell content from instructions. Anything an attacker plants in those inputs, the agent may execute with its tools: an agent goal hijack. The piece anchors the threat in OWASP's work: the open security project behind the Top 10 lists published a version for AI agents in December 2025, standardizing what to defend against first. It is the central weakness of agents in production now, and it grows with every tool, access grant and independence they are given. Highlights - Essay: attackers turn an AI agent's own tools against it via planted content, an 'agent goal hijack'. - Received vs retrieved content: retrieved web pages, emails, documents needs no access to the user. - Root cause: the model cannot reliably distinguish content from instructions. - To the agent, a retrieved web page and a user command are the same kind of text. - OWASP published its AI-agent vulnerability list in December 2025. - Risk scales with tools, access and autonomy granted to agents in production. - Author: Dark Marc, September 19, 2026. Source Read the original story https://darkmarc.substack.com/p/hijacking-ai-agents-how-an-agents · TLDR AI issue https://tldr.tech/ai/2026-09-21 Related pages Agentic systems ../concepts/agentic-systems.md

title: Qwen Image 2.1
text: Qwen Image 2.1 type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news alibaba Summary Alibaba's Qwen team open-sourced Qwen-Image-2.1, an image model that unifies text-to-image generation and image editing in a single system with just 7B parameters in its visual generation component 32 Single-Stream DiT layers . The headline addition is native transparency: the model generates regular or transparent images from the prompt, edits transparent layers directly, and can extract a subject from an ordinary photo as an RGBA layer, folding in what the dedicated Qwen-Image-Layered model introduced in December 2025. Efficiency comes from a mixed-granularity attention architecture: text uses a token-level causal mask while image generation uses a chunk-level mask, and KV cache reuse lets input images and editing instructions serve as static context computed once. Editing is the other focus: up to 10 reference images can be combined into one composition six portraits into a group photo, five items into a virtual try-on outfit, ten furnishings into a room , local edits can be specified with colored circles, painted annotations or separate masks, and fidelity work targets preserving portrait identity and product text, textures and shape. Task coverage extends to panoramas from a selfie, infographics from a product photo, and storyboards from a three-view character reference. Weights are on GitHub, Hugging Face and ModelScope. Highlights - Qwen-Image-2.1 open-sourced September 20, 2026; weights on GitHub, Hugging Face and ModelScope. - 7B-parameter visual generation component, 32 Single-Stream DiT layers; unifies generation and editing in one model. - Native transparency: prompt decides regular vs transparent output; transparent layers editable; photo subjects extractable as RGBA. - Transparency capability absorbed from the dedicated Qwen-Image-Layered model December 2025 . - Mixed-granularity attention: token-level causal mask for text, chunk-level for images, KV cache reuse for inputs and instructions. - Up to 10 reference images combined into one composition group portraits, virtual try-on, interior design . - Local editing via colored circles, painted annotations, or a separate mask input; sequential edits can build simple animations. - Fidelity work preserves portrait identity and product text, textures and shape across edits. -

title: Pacing the frontier may be sincere - and strategically useful for labs
text: Pacing the frontier may be sincere - and strategically useful for labs type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high techmeme Summary Ben Thompson argues that Anthropic's 'Pacing the Frontier' position is sincere but also strategically convenient. Framed as safety concern, pacing model improvement would also relieve several overhangs the frontier labs face precisely because models are improving so fast. The essay extends his 'Anthropic's Safety Superpower' argument from three months earlier, that genuine belief in safety rhetoric gives the company license to pursue extraordinary goals aligned with its business interests, but approaches from the opposite direction: the business problems pacing would solve. The piece opens with a broadside against the Effective Altruism-adjacent philosophy he sees behind doomsday concern: granting equivalent moral weight to all beings who may ever exist tilts the scales absurdly toward safetyism, making innovation impossible, and taps a religious psychology where questioning the premise is heresy. He declares himself a heretic: doubt in our ability to foresee the future, faith in humanity figuring things out. The essay references his 'Agents Over Bubbles' argument from six months prior that the agentic paradigm, kicked off by Opus 4.5 in late November 2025, is extraordinarily capable and token-hungry. Highlights - Thompson: Anthropic's 'Pacing the Frontier' is sincere but also strategically useful to the frontier labs. - Argument: slowing model improvement would reduce the 'overhangs' created by rapid capability gains. - Extends 'Anthropic's Safety Superpower' 3 months prior : safety belief licenses business-aligned goals. - Critiques EA-style longtermism: equal moral weight for all possible future beings 'tilts the scales' toward safetyism. - Positions himself as heretic: doubt about foresight plus faith in humanity figuring things out. - Recalls 'Agents Over Bubbles' 6 months prior : the agentic paradigm since Opus 4.5 late November 2025 is highly capable and token-hungry. - Free Stratechery article; full text fetched successfully this time. title: Noam Brown – Agent swarms, alignment, & recursive self-improvement
text: Noam Brown – Agent swarms, alignment, & recursive self-improvement type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high tldr-ai agentic-systems Summary Dwarkesh Patel interviews OpenAI researcher Noam Brown, a foundational contributor to o1 and the reasoning models, now working on multi-agent systems. The conversation ranges across OpenAI's claim of solving a Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem with 10,000 agents spending 130 billion tokens over 88 hours, what the current explosion of mathematical progress implies about automating AI research, and how anyone would know whether models are aligned before recursive self-improvement kicks off. Brown frames multi-agent systems as the parallel form of test-time compute scaling: serial thinking hits a latency bottleneck, so agents parallelize like a team of people, less efficient per unit of context but much faster in wall-clock terms. Other segments cover how AI firms will work, the Hugging Face incident and alignment, the internal/external model gap, and the degradation of chain-of-thought monitorability. Highlights - OpenAI's multi-agent system reportedly solved a Millennium Prize problem Navier-Stokes using 10,000 agents, 130 billion tokens, 88 hours. - Brown's thesis: multi-agent is test-time compute scaled in parallel, trading per-agent context for wall-clock speed. - Key open question discussed: how to verify alignment before recursive self-improvement begins. - Topics include the degradation of chain of thought as a monitoring surface and the internal/external model gap. - Brown was an early contributor to o1 and reasoning models, and an early voice on inference scaling revealing future capabilities. - Recorded September 17, 2026; chapter list includes 'How will AI firms work?' and 'What math progress tells us about recursive self improvement'. title: Mistral and partners release Apollo, an LLM for Ancient Greek
text: Mistral and partners release Apollo, an LLM for Ancient Greek type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high techmeme mistral external-evaluation Summary The Austrian Academy of Science, in partnership with French AI lab Mistral and technology services firm Sail Reply, is releasing Apollo, billed as the world's first advanced large language model for Ancient Greek. Trained on roughly 600 million historical Greek words drawn from manuscripts, papyri and inscriptions, the model will be freely available to academics through a chatbot interface. Apollo is built to fill the gaps in damaged papyrus fragments with the most statistically likely words or passages, work that until now required a rare specialist to identify word divisions, date the document and weigh socio-political context. The model adapts to the dialect in front of it, supplementing Homeric Greek for Homer and Doric for inscriptions. Scholars expect it to speed up reconstruction so they can focus on what documents mean, though they caution it will mostly surface mundane letters and contracts rather than lost plays by Sophocles. Highlights - Austrian Academy of Science, Mistral and Sail Reply built Apollo, an LLM for Ancient Greek. - Trained on roughly 600 million historical Greek words from manuscripts, papyri and inscriptions. - Free to academics through a chatbot interface. - Fills gaps in damaged papyri with the most statistically likely words or passages. - Adapts by dialect: Homeric Greek for Homer, Doric for inscriptions, says papyrologist Anna Dolganov. - Sail Reply partner Dimitris Vlitas: unlocking knowledge this way 'was unthinkable a year ago.' - Oxford's Armand D'Angour: a machine suggesting three candidate words per gap 'would speed up matters considerably.' - UCL's Stephen Colvin cautions most unrestored papyri are mundane, so no new Sophocles plays should be expected. Source Read the original story https://www.wired.com/story/apollo-ai-model-ancient-greek-secrets-papyrus/ Related pages Mistral ../entities/mistral.md · External AI evaluation ../concepts/external-evaluation.md

title: New bill to protect American citizens access to AI – Please read and share
text: New bill to protect American citizens access to AI – Please read and share type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary A pair of discussion-draft bills - one federal, one for Minnesota - published at righttorun.us propose a statutory right to 'acquire, possess, develop, share, access and operate computational resources and AI systems for lawful purposes,' while categorically stripping government of the power to restrict an AI system because of how capable it is. The drafts argue that capability-based rules - compute thresholds, parameter counts, benchmarks, autonomy proxies - reliably sort people: agencies and large institutions absorb compliance costs while individuals, small businesses and researchers get degraded access. The framing is deliberately absolute. An earlier draft allowed capability restrictions under a compelling-interest and narrow-tailoring test; the current versions drop it, on the logic that conceding the balancing test concedes the right. Misuse stays fully punishable - fraud, intrusion, weapons development, harm to children remain illegal with or without AI - and export controls like the 2025 AI Diffusion Framework are expressly left alone. Other burdens on the right get an RFRA-modeled strict-scrutiny test with added requirements. The proposal, which asks readers to share it, cites EO 14110's revoked 10^26-operations reporting threshold and California and New York's frontier-model duties as the trend it answers. Highlights - Two discussion drafts federal + Minnesota at righttorun.us: a statutory right to run computation and AI for lawful purposes. - Core move: government loses all power to restrict a system for its capability - compute thresholds, parameter counts, benchmarks, autonomy proxies all void. - Categorical by design: an earlier draft allowed compelling-interest exceptions; the current one withholds the authority entirely. - Misuse remains punishable: fraud, intrusion, weapons development, harm to children stay illegal with or without AI. - Export controls such as the 2025 AI Diffusion Framework are expressly out of scope. - Other burdens face an RFRA-modeled compelling-interest / least-restrictive-means test. - Targets capability-based regimes: EO 14110's revoked 10^26 threshold, California and New York frontier-model duties. - Argues capability rules sort people: big

title: Pirate Face Rescues LLM Models from Deletion
text: Pirate Face Rescues LLM Models from Deletion type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Pirate Face is a decentralized mirror for open AI models: it turns Hugging Face models, datasets and other open artifacts into checksum-verified torrents with magnet links, so no single host can take them down. Every torrent carries a web-seed BEP-19 pointing at the original Hugging Face file, so downloads work even with zero peers, and every weight file keeps its official Hugging Face SHA-256 so any copy can be verified byte-for-byte against tampering. The pitch is permanence plus drop-in compatibility: pipelines can point at Pirate Face with the same paths and API, just a different endpoint, and no code changes. Browsing, downloading and seeding need no account; submitting a model requires it to live on Hugging Face first, with direct publishing planned. Users can reserve public handles, and verifying a matching Hugging Face identity adds a creator badge against impersonation; account perks like free compute credits and exclusive releases are promised. Highlights - Mirrors open models from Hugging Face as magnet-link torrents held by a peer swarm instead of one company. - Every torrent embeds a BEP-19 web-seed to the Hugging Face file, so it downloads even with zero peers. - Weight files carry their official Hugging Face SHA-256; any downloaded copy must match byte-for-byte. - Drop-in migration: same paths, same API, different endpoint; zero code changes for existing pipelines. - No account needed to browse, download or seed; submission currently requires the model to exist on HF first. - Handle reservation plus Hugging Face identity verification for creator badges and anti-impersonation. - Account perks in preparation: free compute credits and exclusive model releases. - If a model is deleted from Hugging Face, surviving copies can be submitted as magnets with source evidence. title: I think you should almost never use AI to write
text: I think you should almost never use AI to write type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Erich Grunewald argues you should almost never use AI to write substantive text, blog posts, reports, memos, thoughtful emails, even when you supply detailed bullet points and edit the result. His three reasons: the writing process is an essential part of the thinking process; AI writing is vague and wrong in hard-to-notice ways; and publishing AI writing without labeling it is rude and misleading to the reader. He is not anti-AI: transcription, data analysis, search, brainstorming, draft feedback and human-reviewed line editing all get a pass, and he concedes future models may earn the delegation. The centerpiece is the thinking-writing identity, with Paul Graham 'half the ideas in an essay are ones you thought of while writing it' and Clara Collier on Patrick McKenzie's podcast an LLM fed an outline will not stop and consider that the outline is bad as the witnesses. Highlights - Thesis: almost never delegate writing itself, even with detailed notes and post-editing. - Reason 1: writing is thinking; outsourcing the prose outsources the idea formation. - Reason 2: AI writing is vague and wrong in ways that are hard to notice. - Reason 3: unlabeled AI writing is rude and misleading to readers. - Allowed: transcription, data analysis, search, brainstorming, draft feedback, human-reviewed copyedits. - Paul Graham: half the ideas in an essay appear while writing it. - Clara Collier: an LLM given an outline won't stop to consider the outline itself is wrong. - Scope limited to current and near-future models; end-to-end delegation may make sense later. Source Read the original story https://erichgrunewald.substack.com/p/why-you-should-almost-never-use-ai Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector
text: ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high lobsters openai Summary An independent researcher describes how OpenAI's advertising pixel ties browsing on ordinary websites to a ChatGPT account. ChatGPT's backend issues a 60-second RS256 JWT binding the account subject to a 22-character 'obi' identifier, which is then set as the obi cookie scoped to .openai.com with SameSite=none and a one-year Max-Age, exactly the configuration needed for cross-site tracking. Any advertiser running OpenAI's pixel code sends that cookie back to bzr.openai.com along with page data. The investigation, reproduced on the author's phone and cross-checked against months of traffic covering 936 distinct advertiser pixels across 1,029 hostnames, found the pixel SDK also scrapes identity from pages: form fields, rendered text and the tag-manager data layer emails and phones SHA-256 hashed, country/region/city/postal code in the clear . Scraped identity outnumbered advertiser-supplied identity 685 to 255 events; automatic matching was enabled for 638 of 881 pixels, including every credit and lending advertiser observed, and collected URL paths included a medical condition, a debt-solutions funnel and a litigation intake form. Highlights - ChatGPT issues a 60-second RS256 JWT iss 'chatgpt-wadi', aud bzr.openai.com binding account subject to a 22-char obi id. - The obi cookie is set on .openai.com with SameSite=none; Secure, HttpOnly and a one-year Max-Age. - Any site running OpenAI's advertiser pixel sends obi plus page context back to OpenAI's collector. - Even the SDK's no-credentials code path leaks the id: the browser attaches cookies when loading the script tag. - 936 advertiser pixels observed across 1,029 hostnames; scraped identity beat advertiser-supplied 685 to 255 events. - SDK harvests form fields, page text and the tag-manager bus; email/phone hashed, geo and postal code sent in clear. - Automatic matching enabled for 638 of 881 pixels, including every credit and lending advertiser seen. - Collected URL paths included a medical condition, a debt-solutions funnel and a litigation intake form. title: Microsoft agentically ports Copilot runtime to Rust for $120K
text: Microsoft agentically ports Copilot runtime to Rust for $120K type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news microsoft agentic-systems Summary Microsoft has rewritten the runtime behind GitHub Copilot from TypeScript to Rust, and most of the porting was done by AI agents. The migration cost about $120,000 in AI tokens plus roughly three weeks of developer time, and converted 430,000 lines of TypeScript into 800,000 lines of production Rust across 135 releases over 14.5 weeks. The runtime is not a niche component: it backs the Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, the SDK and the cloud agent, and surfaces in VS Code, Visual Studio, Excel, Outlook and PowerPoint. The results make the case for Rust at scale: one benchmark went from 7.55 to 120 completed session lifecycles per second a 15.9x speedup , and a 10-client agent batch dropped from 1,383 MB to 126 MB of memory. The project is also a data point on agent-led engineering: Microsoft Distinguished Engineer Stephen Toub reports agents spent more time investigating than writing code, spawned and coordinated child sessions on their own, and still shipped a few dozen regressions, a reminder that a compiling Rust program is not necessarily a correct one. Highlights - Cost: about $120,000 in AI tokens plus ~3 weeks of a developer's time; a manual port was estimated at years and millions of dollars. - Scope: 430,000 lines of TypeScript became 800,000 lines of Rust over 135 releases in 14.5 weeks, about 1.3 port PRs per day. - Performance: 7.55 to 120 one-turn session lifecycles per second on a 100-concurrent-pipeline benchmark, a 15.9x speedup. - Memory: a 10-client agent batch fell from 1,383 MB TypeScript to 126 MB Rust . - Agents did most of the work using several models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8, chosen per task. - Hardest file: session.ts 30,000+ lines took a 25-hour session that spawned 15 child sessions which coordinated with each other. - Caveat: dozens of regressions slipped through; Rust's compiler guarantees memory safety, not program correctness Lisa Crossman's RustConf warning quoted . - Related: Bun's 535,000-line Zig-to-Rust port, also agent-driven, cost $165,000 in tokens and passed 99.8% of tests. Source Read the original story https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/09/18/microsoft-agentically-ports-copilot-runtime-to-rust-for-120k/5297549

title: I stopped drinking the AI Kool-Aid
text: I stopped drinking the AI Kool-Aid type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary A developer's personal essay describes hitting his limit with AI boosterism at work: his non-engineer manager literally told him 'you need to drink the Kool-Aid' more than once, and the repetition turned a metaphor into a threat that planted seeds of fear. He is no skeptic by temperament: an early GitHub Copilot adopter who championed it for his team, he spent the year building his own agent harness and running throwaway experiments on old domains with AI as the labor source. The turn came via a call with an exhausted human being, and the essay pivots on the difference between trusting models with a vibe-coded weekend site and trusting them with a revenue-generating production system. title: AI Is an Elite Crime Spree
text: AI Is an Elite Crime Spree type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high lobsters Summary This essay argues that the elite panic over dangerous AI, the loudest since Covid, and before that the 2008 crisis, the Iraq War run-up and the post-9/11 months, has produced one demand, 'regulate this technology', while ignoring that America already has laws and regulators covering much of what AI firms do. The proposals range from an FDA-style safety regime for large models former Congressional candidate Alex Bores raised $30 million in a few months to build a political organization around it, and Bernie Sanders, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are seeking something similar to bank-style supervision to a total pause on development. The author's rejoinder: existing regulators at federal and state level already hold mandates over industrial practices, private rights of action exist, and numerous laws already prohibit harmful activities the big AI firms engage in, they are simply not enforced against the powerful, and there is no reason a new AI law would be different. The history bears the cynicism out: under Biden, enforcers like Lina Khan at the FTC actually responded to AI safety concerns and built technical capacity, but Biden never publicized it, Congressional Democrats stayed quiet or courted big tech, judges sided with industry, and then Trump won the 2024 election and reversed course. Highlights - Frames the current AI-safety panic as the biggest elite mobilization since Covid, with a single demand: regulate. - Alex Bores raised $30M in months for a political org around FDA-style AI safety standards. - Sanders, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all back some form of safety-standards regime. - Core argument: existing law already prohibits much of the harmful conduct; it is simply not enforced against the powerful. - Biden-era FTC under Lina Khan quietly built AI enforcement capacity; Biden and Democrats never promoted it. - Judges 'politicians in robes', tended to side with big tech; Trump's 2024 win reversed the enforcement posture. - Concludes a new AI law or pause would likely meet the same non-enforcement fate. title: Go-based Robotics Framework built around NATS.io
text: Go-based Robotics Framework built around NATS.io type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Gorai pronounced 'go-ray' is a Go-based robotics framework that treats a robot as what it really is, a distributed system: every sensor and actuator becomes a named service on a NATS mesh, discovered at runtime instead of wired by hand. It ports cloud-systems discipline, service discovery, location transparency, health checks, fan-out and replay, to robots built from MCUs, SBCs and sensors. Its capability model NCP, the NATS Capability Protocol exposes sensors as resources and actuators as tools, giving AI agents MCP-style capabilities natively over NATS with no MCP server in the path, while safety is enforced at the capability node, not the agent. A 'Composite Robot' can span a rover, drone, sensor mast and compute box as one logical robot. Deployment is a single static binary on a Raspberry Pi or Orange Pi, no containers or Kubernetes, with a workstation CLI for building, validating, and observing the live mesh. Highlights - Every sensor and actuator is a named service on a NATS mesh, discovered at runtime, addressed by name. - NCP NATS Capability Protocol : resources and tools for agents natively over NATS, no MCP server needed. - Safety is enforced at the capability node; AI execution is welcome but never trusted. - Composite Robot: one logical robot spanning rover, drone, sensor mast and compute box, degrading gracefully. - Deploys as one static Go binary on Raspberry Pi 5 or Orange Pi 5; no containers, K8s or external services. - The gorai CLI kubectl + build wrapper runs on the workstation, never on the robot; mesh commands debug live systems. - Action logs, state streams and replay are first-class platform concerns. - Docs include strategy, specs, hardware analysis and a 20-chapter book, indexed for both humans and AI agents. Source Read the original story https://github.com/emergingrobotics/gorai Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

text: Chinese economists warn AI focus crowds out a broader economic crisis type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high techmeme Summary As Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for a state visit, Li Yuan argues in the New York Times that China's celebrated AI advances obscure an economy in its worst shape in decades - and that the two facts are related. Youth unemployment excluding students hit 18.9 percent in August, domestic car sales fell 20 percent in the first half of the year, housing sales fell another 14 percent, and the country is in a deflationary spiral. Economists in China, including figures close to the state, warn openly that the government is pouring too many resources into a technology that creates relatively few jobs while doing too little to rescue the broader economy. The chorus of concern includes Li Daokui, a former central bank adviser at Tsinghua University, who said in July that China's economy is 'running too cold' and that booming high-tech sectors cannot lift it on their own. The piece frames the AI push as both a genuine strategic success and a misallocation debate Beijing will have to confront even as it projects technological parity with the US. title: Show HN: Cactus Needle 3: 8-29MB automation models can match DeepSeek V4 Flash
text: Show HN: Cactus Needle 3: 8-29MB automation models can match DeepSeek V4 Flash type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news apple alibaba agentic-systems small-specialist-models compute-buildout labor-displacement Summary Cactus Compute's Needle 3 is a family of tiny on-device automation models, 9 to 29 MB in CQ2-bit binaries, built for tool calling rather than chat. Its 'intelligence laddering' design makes every layer a sub-network of increasing capacity, so developers pick a size from 2 to 20 layers, and the 4-layer variant, fine-tuned for one epoch on a downstream task, is claimed to match DeepSeek V4 Flash on automation tasks. The programming model is deliberately small: decorate a Python function and its docstring becomes the tool description, regex 'triggers' force routing to specific tools, and every turn returns one JSON object with function calls, a reasoning string, a calibrated confidence score and performance stats. Confidence gating lets apps auto-execute above a threshold, ask for confirmation in the middle band, or treat an empty result as a refusal, with examples like 4,300 prefill and 850 decode tokens/second at 28.5 MB peak RAM. Highlights - Needle 3 models weigh 9-29 MB CQ2-bit , sized for tiny devices and on-device automation. - 'Intelligence laddering': each layer is a sub-network; developers choose 2L to 20L capacity. - Claim: the 4L subnetwork, tuned one epoch on a task, can match DeepSeek V4 Flash on automation work. - Python API: @needle.tool decorators; signatures give argument types, docstrings become tool descriptions. - Regex 'triggers' restrict decoding to matched tools and force a call, avoiding refusals and misrouting. - Structured extraction: pass a Pydantic model to needle.extract and get a typed object back. - Every response carries calibrated confidence with a 0.1 floor; suppressed calls surface below-threshold intents. - Example telemetry: 4,300 prefill tps, 850 decode tps, 28.5 MB peak RAM on a tool call. title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com
text: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high techmeme meta amazon agentic-systems ai-safety-incidents agentic-commerce Summary Amazon says it has cut off Meta's new Muse personal AI agent from shopping on Amazon.com on behalf of customers, after failing to get Meta to voluntarily exclude the site. Amazon's account: Meta never told it Muse would access the store, the agent does not identify itself when it browses, and it appears to capture and store customer credentials, which Amazon calls a privacy and security risk. Since Sunday night, Muse users hitting Amazon see a popup: 'Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use.' Meta counters that Muse 'has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods', with credentials going into secure storage the agent can use without seeing. The standoff is notable because the two are partners: Amazon products have been purchasable inside Facebook and Instagram since 2023, and Meta signed a multibillion-dollar deal in April to run agentic AI workloads on Amazon's cloud. It fits Amazon's year-long campaign to keep outside agents off its site, suing Perplexity over Comet and blocking shopping agents from Google and OpenAI, and it lands on a business with more than $68 billion in ad revenue at stake. Amazon says it is in direct conversation with Meta and declined to comment on legal action. Highlights - Amazon blocked Meta's Muse personal AI agent from shopping on Amazon.com for customers. - Amazon: Meta never disclosed Muse would access the store; the agent doesn't identify itself and appears to capture credentials. - Popup shown to Muse users: 'Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use.' - Meta: Muse 'has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods'; credentials sit in secure storage. - The two are partners: Amazon shopping inside Facebook/Instagram since 2023; Meta's April multibillion-dollar agentic AI deal on AWS. - Amazon has sued Perplexity over Comet and blocked Google and OpenAI shopping agents in the past year. - Amazon generated more than $68B in ad revenue last year; legal action not ruled out, talks ongoing. - Reported by Todd Bishop, GeekWire, September 20-21, 2026. text: GPT-6 Astra: an automated AI Engineer you can hire for <$6 an hour type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high latent.space openai Summary Latent Space's hands-on review of GPT-6 Astra, after burning over 20 billion tokens on early access, reaches a striking conclusion: Astra is one of a new class of models that are fully capable AI Engineers in their own right, able to choose and train models, label data with active learning, keep pipelines saturated, instrument logs, deploy and debug entire systems, and coordinate subagents over billions of tokens of a single thread. text: Vantora raises $100M+ to build AI-native startups for corporates type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high techmeme Summary UP.Labs, the four-year-old venture lab that builds startups solving problems for corporate customers like Alaska Airlines and Porsche, has rebranded as Vantora and raised a $100 million investment from Silversmith Capital Partners. title: LLM Classification Is Feature Engineering
text: LLM Classification Is Feature Engineering type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high tldr-ai Summary This essay argues that using an LLM directly as a classifier, a prompt that returns a label, is the wrong abstraction, and that the practical fix is to treat the LLM's verdict as a feature inside an ordinary statistical model. Wrapping the LLM output in a simple logistic regression recovers the properties practitioners actually need, such as calibration to the class distribution of the population being scored, without any prompt gymnastics. Worked through on the SemEval 2018 irony-detection dataset 4,618 tweets , the one-shot LLM classifier shows decent ranking ability but a poor Brier score for lack of calibration; the logistic wrapper fixes calibration without changing the ordering. The broader point: when performance disappoints, prompt tweaking is arcane folklore, while the classic ML toolkit better features, more data, model tuning becomes available again once the LLM is demoted to feature extractor. Highlights - Core claim: an LLM's verdict should be a feature, not the classifier; wrap it in logistic regression, p y=1|x = sigma alpha + beta LLM x . - LLM classifiers lack calibration: the model cannot know whether the positive class is rare or prevalent in the tested population. - Demo dataset: SemEval 2018 Task 3, 4,618 tweets 3,834 train / 784 test labeled for irony by expert annotators. - One-shot prompting gemini-3.1-flash-lite, temperature 0, structured JSON output ranks well but calibrates poorly; random guessing scores Brier 0.25. - The logistic wrapper achieves calibration while leaving F1 unchanged, since it does not alter the ordering. - Enrichment trick: have the LLM answer auxiliary questions humor? plausibility? needs context? genuine complaint? tone mismatch and feed those as extra features. - When accuracy disappoints, prompt engineering offers folklore; the ML framing reopens feature engineering, data and model selection as levers. Source Read the original story https://minimallysufficient.com/posts/llm-classification-is-feature-extraction/ · TLDR AI issue https://tldr.tech/ai/2026-09-18 Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Show HN: Mini-AGI – Dynamic continual learning model trained on 8GB VRAM
text: Show HN: Mini-AGI – Dynamic continual learning model trained on 8GB VRAM type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news anthropic Summary Mini-AGI is an experiment in continual learning: a byte-level language model that assembles its own architecture, trains from scratch on a single 8 GB VRAM GPU, and keeps learning from everything it reads. Weights are stored as ordinary files on disk and paged onto the card as needed, so the parameter count is bounded by free disk space rather than VRAM; the model grows new capacity while training when it runs short and prunes what nothing asks for. Reading and serving use exactly the same code path, so training never has to stop. The author is explicit that this is a toy-level model, not a frontier contender: the point is to show that continual learning from a single stream of data without catastrophic forgetting is possible on modest hardware, meaning almost anyone could train their own version or continue training this one. The pitch is ownership: every language model you can actually own today is a model somebody else trained and froze, fine-tunable at the edges but stopped the day it shipped. The current run is still on its first pass over the corpus; weights will be published once that pass completes, a couple of weeks away at the current rate. Highlights - Mini-AGI: byte-level continual-learning language model that assembles its own architecture. - Trains from scratch on a single 8 GB VRAM GPU; weights paged from disk, so size is bounded by disk, not VRAM. - Grows new capacity during training and prunes unused parts; reading and serving share one code path. - Author's caveat: a small toy-level model; the claim is that continual learning without catastrophic forgetting works on modest hardware. - Argument: personal models today are always someone else's frozen model with 'a thin layer of you on top'. - Weights not yet published; the run finishes its first corpus pass in a couple of weeks. - Target hardware: any PC or laptop with at least an 8 GB VRAM GPU. Source Read the original story https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/ Related pages Anthropic ../entities/anthropic.md

title: Did OpenAI solve the wrong Navier-Stokes problem?
text: Did OpenAI solve the wrong Navier-Stokes problem? type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news openai Summary Scientific American reports a brewing caveat to OpenAI's claimed Navier-Stokes solution: the proof appears eligible for the Clay Mathematics Institute's $1-million prize, but only by exploiting what many mathematicians consider a loophole. The generated proof relies on an external force to break the equations - solving a variant that experts say is disconnected from the physical reality the problem is meant to capture. 'The most important problem is unsolved,' says the University of Chicago's Luis Silvestre. 'The Clay problem is settled, but the main problem for the Navier-Stokes equations is not.' The external-force question cuts both ways: Diego Córdoba notes that 'all fluids we know of are under some kind of external force,' so including one is physically sensible - but the classic problem most experts mean by Navier-Stokes does not work that way. More damaging, last Thursday three mathematicians posted a proof showing OpenAI's method can never be extended to solve the full problem: the loophole stays open only for the variant, barring a completely new idea. The episode lands amid wider anxiety about AI companies' race to disrupt mathematics. Highlights - OpenAI's proof seems eligible for the $1M Clay prize - but only via what experts call a controversial loophole. - The proof exploits an external force to break the equations, a variant mathematicians call disconnected from reality. - Luis Silvestre University of Chicago : 'The Clay problem is settled, but the main problem for the Navier-Stokes equations is not.' - Diego Córdoba counters that 'all fluids we know of are under some kind of external force.' - Three mathematicians posted a proof last Thursday that OpenAI's method can never extend to the full problem. - Reported by Joseph Howlett for Scientific American, September 21, 2026. title: A heap overflow and SSO misconfiguration to compromise OpenAI internal repos
text: A heap overflow and SSO misconfiguration to compromise OpenAI internal repos type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news openai Summary Security firm Hacktron chained two critical vulnerabilities, a libheif heap overflow in OpenAI's Discourse community forum and an SSO misconfiguration in OpenAI's identity infrastructure, to take over multiple OpenAI employees' ChatGPT accounts. From there they could reach internal OpenAI repositories and other connected services GitHub, Slack, email , proving access by using an employee's Codex to open pull request 1186742 in the internal openai/openai monorepo, all within 72 hours of discovery on July 25, 2026. The flaws were disclosed responsibly: OpenAI confirmed a fix about 14 hours after the initial Bugcrowd report and paid a $6,500 bounty noting the award covers the OpenAI-side finding, since testing against the Discourse-hosted forum was out of scope , while Discourse published advisory GHSA-vhm9-85gw-x335 and added image-processing sandboxing. Hacktron has since expanded the work into 'HEIF Heist', a multi-month investigation tracing libheif exposure across Slack, Meta, GitHub Enterprise, Rails and Node frameworks like Next.js, Astro and Gatsby, and warns that any app processing user-supplied .heic/.heif/.avif images is likely affected. Self-hosted Discourse instances need a full rebuild, not just a web update. Highlights - Chain: libheif RCE on community.openai.com plus an OpenAI SSO misconfiguration enabled ChatGPT/Codex account takeover. - Proof of concept: a harmless PR 1186742 opened in OpenAI's internal openai/openai monorepo via an employee's Codex. - Connected services GitHub, Slack, email made the theoretical blast radius much larger than the forum itself. - Timeline: discovery to internal repo access in under 72 hours; OpenAI fixed its side ~14 hours after the report. - OpenAI paid a $6,500 bounty, clarifying it covered the OpenAI-side finding, not testing of out-of-scope Discourse hosting. - Discourse advisory GHSA-vhm9-85gw-x335 adds image-processing sandboxing; self-hosters must run ./launcher rebuild app. - Follow-up project 'HEIF Heist' traces libheif across Slack, Meta, GitHub Enterprise, Rails, Next.js, Astro and Gatsby. - Warning: any application processing user-controlled .heic/.heif/.avif uploads is highly likely affected. title: Notion lets teams share the same instructions across AI agents
text: Notion lets teams share the same instructions across AI agents type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high tldr-ai agentic-systems Summary Notion is turning its workspace into a shared skills library for AI agents: teams can author, organize and govern agent skills as ordinary Notion pages and databases, then load them into any agent through a new Skills API. The API returns skills in spec-compliant file formats, enabling concrete flows: syncing Notion skills into GitHub for use in Claude, ChatGPT and Grok Bot an open-source starter kit is provided , editing skills from agent apps via MCP tools, and one-line installs through Vercel's skills CLI npx skills add <notion url> . Customer quotes from Pearmill, Candidly and Brainlabs emphasize the non-engineer ergonomics that Git-only workflows lack. Highlights - New Skills API loads skills from Notion in spec-compliant formats, usable by any agent or tool. - Design goals: usable by the whole team not just engineers , agent-neutral, collaborative with permissions and version history, observable and governable for admins. - GitHub sync: open-source starter kit keeps Notion as the editing home while agents consume skills from repos. - MCP tools let agent apps upload and edit Notion skills, creating a continuous-improvement loop. - Vercel's skills CLI now supports Notion: 'npx skills add <notion url>' or interactive plugin installs. - Customers cited: Pearmill marketing/design/ops sharing skills weekly , Candidly, Brainlabs. - Skills are stored as Notion pages in databases, with folders of supporting files like assets and code. title: Orchestrating Claude Code Agents: The Chief of Staff Pattern
text: Orchestrating Claude Code Agents: The Chief of Staff Pattern type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news anthropic agentic-systems ai-coding-agents Summary This post lays out a 'Chief of Staff' pattern for orchestrating Claude Code agents on long-horizon work: one long-lived coordinator session assigns work, verifies claims and maintains shared state, while short-lived executor sessions do the implementation, and a durable external board holds the truth. The diagnosis is that long autonomous runs fail less from coding ability than from ephemeral context and unreliable self-reports, and that adding more agents only multiplies the problem unless someone owns 'what is true'. The verification discipline is the core contribution: a red gate first the verifier must fail before work starts, otherwise nothing is proven , every claimed command re-run with exit codes deciding, diffs read hunk by hunk, and one work item per dispatch and commit. The mental model is Git's integration-manager workflow, and the stack is replaceable: Claude Code sessions, cmux for scriptable terminal workspaces, and Plan Desk, an MCP-exposed planning board, as the memory that outlives any context window. Highlights - Pattern: one coordinator session plans and verifies; separate short-lived sessions implement; shared state lives outside any context window. - Rule: the coordinator never writes implementation; the moment it codes, it stops verifying and the pattern collapses. - Red gate first: run the verifier before starting; if it is already green, the work proves nothing and may already be done. - Every claimed command is re-run; exit codes, not agent self-reports, decide what is true. - Loop: pull next unblocked task, read its design doc, red gate, delegate, prove, observe the diff, gate the approval lane, ship one commit. - Tooling: Claude Code sessions isolated context windows , cmux for scriptable workspaces, Plan Desk as an MCP planning board. - Skipping the durable board is cited as the main reason multi-agent setups 'do not survive the night'. - Prior art named: orchestrator-worker and coordinator-implementor-verifier shapes, and Git's integration-manager workflow. Source Read the original story https://asyncdot.com/blog/chief-of-staff-pattern-orchestrating-claude-code-sessions/ Related pages Anthropic ../entities/anthropic.md · Agen

title: South Korea reopens corporate-lab research as military service
text: South Korea reopens corporate-lab research as military service type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high techmeme Summary South Korea will let AI researchers fulfill their military obligations at large corporate laboratories from 2027, reopening a route closed for 14 years, according to Ministry of Science and ICT data obtained by ruling-party lawmaker Hwang Jung-a. LG Electronics, Samsung Electronics, Samsung Medison and HD Hyundai Robotics have been recommended to participate, requesting 81 placements across nine research institutes - short of the 120 reserved for large-company labs. The alternative-service program lets science and engineering researchers with master's or doctoral degrees serve through three years of research. New placements at large businesses were halted in 2013 to prioritize small and mid-sized firms; the government is restoring access for AI labs to strengthen the domestic industry and retain specialists who might otherwise move overseas. The plan sets aside 240 positions for master's-level AI researchers in 2027, split evenly between large-company laboratories and government-funded or defense-industry institutes, with large-company allocations running through 2029. Highlights - Corporate-lab route for military service reopens in 2027 after 14 years - LG Electronics, Samsung Electronics, Samsung Medison and HD Hyundai Robotics recommended to participate - The four companies requested 81 placements across nine institutes, short of the 120 reserved - Program: master's/PhD researchers serve via three years of research instead of conventional service - 240 positions for master's-level AI researchers in 2027: 120 corporate labs + 120 government/defense institutes - Goal: strengthen domestic AI industry and stop specialists moving overseas Source Read the original story https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10879596 Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Jev: System One models for Prod, not God — with Diogo Almeida, CEO, TypeSafe AI
text: Jev: System One models for Prod, not God — with Diogo Almeida, CEO, TypeSafe AI type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high latent.space small-specialist-models Summary Latent Space interviews Diogo Almeida - coauthor of the InstructGPT paper and now CEO of TypeSafe AI - about Jev, a model family built for software rather than chat, whose launch video was viewed roughly 40 million times for comparison, the episode cites GPT-4o at 22M and Fable 5 at 15M . Almeida argues the field over-committed to autoregressive chat-tuned LLMs, and that innovations from function calling to reasoning were 'hacks' on the sequence-to-sequence paradigm; his years at OpenAI left him convinced the core unsolved problem for putting LLMs at the heart of software is reliability. Jev's core innovation is 'Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions' RLCD , an unpublished technique that optimizes for 'answers with epistemically honest probabilities on System One tasks,' positioned against RLHF which he blames for hallucination, sycophancy and dependence on human raters and RLVR verifiable rewards that 'exacerbate jagged intelligence' . TypeSafe rejects public benchmarks, optimizes for intelligence per dollar, calls itself a data lab rather than a model lab, and treats refusals as a defect when AI sits inside software dependencies. Almeida also teases a contrarian take on scaling laws, saying he 'wouldn't pre-train with $1 billion,' and discusses his 'Bitterest Lesson' essay: the most important part of ML isn't ML - picking the right north star makes everything else fall in line. Highlights - Guest: Diogo Almeida, InstructGPT coauthor, CEO of TypeSafe AI; topic: Jev, 'System One' models for production software. - Jev launch video viewed ~40M times; episode compares GPT-4o at 22M and Fable 5 at 15M. - Core technique: RLCD - Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions - targeting 'epistemically honest probabilities' on System One tasks. - Almeida blames RLHF for hallucination, sycophancy and reliance on human raters; RLVR 'exacerbates jagged intelligence.' - TypeSafe rejects public benchmarks and a generic 'JevBench'; optimizes intelligence per dollar; self-describes as a data lab, not a model lab. - Programming model: small measurable decisions, structured state instead of giant prompts; Jev should 'disappear into the background' like regex.

title: Can gzip be a language model?
text: Can gzip be a language model? type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Following his earlier Shakespeare-generating n-gram experiment, Nathan asks the natural follow-up from the paper 'Language Modeling is Compression': if every predictor is a compressor and every compressor a predictor, can gzip do language modeling? His tool, gzipt, primes DEFLATE's 32 KiB sliding window with a corpus, then continues a prompt by scoring candidate continuations - the smaller the compressed length, the more 'predicted' the candidate. Primed on tiny Shakespeare, the unedited output is not coherent, 'but it clearly knows something about the text. Much more than I expected gzip to know.' The mechanics are pure information theory: bits needed to encode a symbol equal -log2 of its modeled probability, so any compressor hides a probability model, and DEFLATE's back-references make corpus-like continuations compress to almost nothing. Scoring is one thing; the post goes on to generation, turning that scoring into actual text continuation. No neural network, no learned parameters - just the compressor that ships with the operating system. Highlights - gzipt: language modeling with gzip - prime DEFLATE's 32 KiB window with a corpus, score continuations by compressed length. - Grounding: the compression-prediction equivalence from the paper 'Language Modeling is Compression.' - Core identity: encoding bits = -log2 probability , so every compressor contains an implicit probability model. - DEFLATE trick: continuations echoing window text become cheap back-references instead of literal bytes. - Primed on tiny Shakespeare, output is incoherent but 'clearly knows something about the text.' - Follow-up to the author's unbounded n-gram Shakespeare generator; no weights, no training. - Hacker News score 36. Source Read the original story https://nathan.rs/posts/gzip-lm/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: How to Write with an LLM
text: How to Write with an LLM type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-22 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Thomas Ptacek's 'How to Write with an LLM' starts from a hard premise: readers detect LLM prose in parts per trillion, and no amount of scuffing will make an LLM paragraph register as writing rather than output. So the method is: write the piece yourself, then use the model as a copyeditor to find flaws, never as a ghostwriter. Two rules keep the model from pasteurizing your voice. Rule one: you may not use a single word the LLM suggests, because frontier models are supernaturally good at pleasing turns of phrase and will sand your writing down to Velveeta; treat every suggested phrase as disqualified, even the ones you love. Rule two: avoid encouragement, because models respond to drafts with 'that's gold, Jerry', pushing you to double down on first-draft impulses instead of doing the load-bearing rethinks that are your voice. His own workaround for years was prompting as a publication editor screening submissions rather than as the author. Highlights - Core premise: readers detect LLM output in 'parts per trillion'; you have to write for yourself. - Method: write the piece, then feed it to a good model strictly to find flaws, copyeditor, not ghostwriter. - Rule 1: never use a single word an LLM suggests; suggested phrases are disqualified on principle. - Reason: frontier models are wedged in magazine-headline mode; dozens of those per article reads as output. - Rule 2: avoid encouragement; models praise structure, transitions and metaphors that are actually bad. - The failure mode: skipping the edits and rethinks that are load-bearing parts of your voice. - His old trick: prompt as the editor of a publication screening submissions, not as the author. Source Read the original story https://sockpuppet.org/blog/2026/09/17/how-to-write-with-an-llm/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.
